PV power plant design: a small multi-objective study¶

Goal: learn basic pvlib modeling, then explore energy–cost–variability trade-offs using NSGA-II.

We design a hypothetical fixed-tilt, 10–100 kWp installation in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Tilt varies from 0–60° and azimuth from 90–270° (90° east, 180° south, 270° west). The baseline is 10°, south-facing, 50 kWp.

Run cells in order using Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells. See README.md for installation and the full guide. The checked weather cache permits offline reruns after installing dependencies.

1. What pvlib does¶

pvlib python is an open-source library for modeling photovoltaic systems. It converts location, weather, and system specifications into estimated electrical output.

The workflow here is:

Weather + solar position → irradiance on the tilted panels → cell temperature → DC power → inverter AC power → energy

pvlib API Role in this project
iotools.get_pvgis_tmy() Retrieve historical-derived hourly irradiance, air temperature, and wind
location.Location Store latitude, longitude, elevation, and timezone
Location.get_solarposition() Calculate solar elevation, zenith, and azimuth
pvsystem.PVSystem Describe panel orientation, DC nameplate power, inverter, and thermal parameters
temperature.TEMPERATURE_MODEL_PARAMETERS Supply generic open-rack SAPM temperature coefficients
modelchain.ModelChain.with_pvwatts() Select simple PVWatts electrical models and associated modeling steps
ModelChain.run_model(weather) Run the simulation with a pandas DataFrame
ModelChain.results Inspect panel irradiance, cell temperature, DC power, and AC power

pvlib performs the physical simulation. pandas and NumPy calculate the metrics; pymoo searches designs; Matplotlib draws the figures.

2. Configure the site and experiment¶

The installation is an aggregate generic array. Capacity is continuous in kWp; we do not choose a real panel product or a discrete module count.

The DC/AC ratio is fixed at 1.2, so a 50 kWp DC system uses an inverter with about 41.67 kW AC rating. Keeping this ratio fixed makes power scale linearly with system size under the selected models.

In [2]:
site = Site()
baseline_design = Design(tilt_deg=10, azimuth_deg=180, size_kwp=50)
location = pvlib.location.Location(
    latitude=site.latitude, longitude=site.longitude,
    tz=site.timezone, altitude=site.altitude_m, name=site.name,
)
POPULATION = 40
GENERATIONS = 30
SEED = 42
OUTPUT_DIR = ROOT / "outputs"

display(pd.DataFrame({"variable": DESIGN_COLUMNS,
                      "lower": LOWER_BOUNDS, "upper": UPPER_BOUNDS}))
print(location)
print("Baseline:", baseline_design)

3. Load historical-derived weather¶

load_weather() uses pvlib.iotools.get_pvgis_tmy() on the first run and otherwise reads the local CSV and metadata. It verifies the source location, checksum, required columns, finite values, and 8,760 consecutive local hours.

TMY means Typical Meteorological Year. Months are selected from different historical years. The 2023 dates are convenient non-leap calendar labels, not a claim that these observations were recorded in 2023. The source database and selected historical months are preserved in the metadata.

The download uses map_variables=True, roll_utc_offset=7, and coerce_year=2023. Rolling to local time preserves 365 complete local days. No synthetic weather is silently substituted.

Irradiance timing: PVGIS ERA5 labels rows at HH:00 but its hourly-average irradiance corresponds to HH:30. The metadata records this 0.5-hour offset. weather_for_model() shifts the simulation timestamps to the midpoint before calculating sun position; the cached CSV keeps its original hour labels. Each value still represents one hour. See the JRC TMY timing documentation.

Column Meaning Unit
ghi Global horizontal irradiance W/m²
dni Direct normal irradiance W/m²
dhi Diffuse horizontal irradiance W/m²
temp_air Ambient air temperature °C
wind_speed Wind speed m/s

4. First pvlib feature: solar position¶

The sun's position depends on location and time. Solar zenith is the angle from vertical; apparent elevation is the height above the horizon, including refraction. pvlib measures azimuth clockwise from north.

This standalone example helps explain a step that ModelChain will later perform internally.

In [4]:
solar_position = location.get_solarposition(model_weather.index)
display(solar_position[["apparent_elevation", "apparent_zenith", "azimuth"]].head())

day = solar_position.loc["2023-03-21"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
day["apparent_elevation"].plot(ax=ax, color="tab:orange")
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=1)
ax.set(title="Solar elevation on a TMY calendar day", ylabel="Elevation (degrees)",
       xlabel="Local time (UTC+7)")

5. Define and simulate the baseline system¶

Here are the main pvlib calls explicitly, before using the shared helper in the optimizer.

  • module_parameters["pdc0"] is aggregate array DC nameplate power in watts.
  • gamma_pdc=-0.004 means about −0.4% DC power per °C above the 25°C reference temperature.
  • The inverter's pdc0 is a DC input reference. Its AC rating is eta_inv_nom × pdc0; the same parameter name has a different meaning in the module model.
  • SAPM temperature coefficients represent open-rack glass/glass modules.
  • Hay–Davies transposition calculates irradiance on the tilted plane; physical incidence-angle losses and PVWatts DC/inverter models are applied.
  • The listed generic loss percentages combine multiplicatively to approximately 14.08%, in addition to temperature, angle-of-incidence, and inverter effects. The shading percentage is a lumped allowance, not a geometric shading simulation.
In [5]:
dc_nameplate_w = baseline_design.size_kwp * 1000
ac_rating_w = dc_nameplate_w / DC_AC_RATIO
thermal_parameters = pvlib.temperature.TEMPERATURE_MODEL_PARAMETERS["sapm"]["open_rack_glass_glass"]

system = pvlib.pvsystem.PVSystem(
    surface_tilt=baseline_design.tilt_deg,
    surface_azimuth=baseline_design.azimuth_deg,
    module_parameters={"pdc0": dc_nameplate_w, "gamma_pdc": -0.004},
    inverter_parameters={"pdc0": ac_rating_w / INVERTER_EFFICIENCY,
                         "eta_inv_nom": INVERTER_EFFICIENCY},
    temperature_model_parameters=thermal_parameters,
    losses_parameters={"soiling": 2, "shading": 3, "snow": 0, "mismatch": 2,
                       "wiring": 2, "connections": 0.5, "lid": 1.5,
                       "nameplate_rating": 1, "age": 0, "availability": 3},
    albedo=0.2,
)
model_chain = pvlib.modelchain.ModelChain.with_pvwatts(
    system, location, transposition_model="haydavies", temperature_model="sapm",
    aoi_model="physical", spectral_model="no_loss",
)
model_chain.run_model(model_weather)
baseline_ac_kw = (model_chain.results.ac / 1000).clip(lower=0).rename("ac_kw")
print(model_chain)
print(f"DC nameplate: {dc_nameplate_w / 1000:.2f} kWp; AC rating: {ac_rating_w / 1000:.2f} kW")

6. Calculate energy and variability¶

Power and energy have different units: kW × hours = kWh. With complete, evenly spaced hourly data, each sample contributes AC_kW × 1 hour.

The relative daily variability measure is:

[ CV_{daily} = \frac{\sigma(E_1,\ldots,E_{365})}{\operatorname{mean}(E_1,\ldots,E_{365})} ]

We use population standard deviation (ddof=0) because these are all days of the representative year. CV is dimensionless: 0.20 means the standard deviation is 20% of mean daily energy.

It captures the spread of daily totals, including seasonal variation. It does not measure hourly ramps, temporal ordering, or interannual uncertainty. Normalization avoids automatically favoring a smaller installation just because its absolute power changes are smaller.

In [7]:
hourly_energy_kwh = baseline_ac_kw * 1.0
daily_energy_kwh = hourly_energy_kwh.resample("D").sum()
monthly_energy_kwh = hourly_energy_kwh.resample("MS").sum()

baseline_metrics = {
    "annual_energy_kwh": float(hourly_energy_kwh.sum()),
    "investment_usd": investment_cost(baseline_design),
    "daily_cv": float(daily_energy_kwh.std(ddof=0) / daily_energy_kwh.mean()),
}
display(pd.Series(baseline_metrics))
print(f"Specific yield: {baseline_metrics['annual_energy_kwh'] / baseline_design.size_kwp:.1f} kWh/kWp")
_ = plot_baseline(weather, baseline_ac_kw, OUTPUT_DIR / "figures")
plt.show()

7. Compare a few designs before optimizing¶

The cost model is deliberately simple:

[ C = 5000 + S,(800 + 2\beta) ]

Here (S) is size in kWp and (\beta) is tilt in degrees. Units of the coefficients are USD, USD/kWp, and USD/(kWp·degree). The tilt term represents an illustrative mounting allowance. These values are teaching assumptions, not market quotations. Orientation affects physical production, but has no direct cost term.

The shared PVSimulator uses the same pvlib configuration as the explicit baseline above. It simulates a 1 kWp reference and scales it because size and inverter rating change together. It caches exact orientation pairs without rounding design variables.

In [8]:
simulator = PVSimulator(weather, site)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    simulator.power(baseline_design).to_numpy(), baseline_ac_kw.to_numpy(),
    rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-10,
)

examples = {
    "Baseline": baseline_design,
    "East-facing": Design(10, 90, 50),
    "West-facing": Design(10, 270, 50),
    "Steeper tilt": Design(40, 180, 50),
    "Smaller system": Design(10, 180, 10),
    "Larger system": Design(10, 180, 100),
}
comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    label: simulator.evaluate(design) for label, design in examples.items()
}).T
display(comparison[DESIGN_COLUMNS + METRIC_COLUMNS].round(3))

8. Multi-objective optimization with NSGA-II¶

A design dominates another when it is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in at least one. A Pareto set contains designs not dominated by the other candidates.

pymoo minimizes objectives, so the objective vector is:

[-annual_energy_kwh, investment_usd, daily_cv]

NSGA-II creates a population, ranks it by dominance, preserves diversity using crowding distance, and generates new candidates through crossover and mutation. We run 40 designs over 30 generations with a fixed seed. This is an educational computational budget, not proof of global convergence.

PVDesignProblem._evaluate() calls simulator.evaluate(Design(...)) and returns the three objectives. optimize_designs() calls pymoo's NSGA2 and minimize. The initial population includes the baseline and two boundary-size examples. The reported approximate Pareto set is filtered from all candidates evaluated during this run, rather than only the final population.

In [10]:
pareto, evaluated, optimization_result = optimize_designs(
    simulator, population=POPULATION, generations=GENERATIONS,
    seed=SEED, verbose=True,
)
print(f"Evaluated {len(evaluated):,} designs; retained {len(pareto):,} nondominated designs.")
print("pymoo final population size:", len(optimization_result.pop))
display(pareto.head().round(3))

9. Visualize the trade-offs¶

Each colored point is a nondominated evaluated design. Gray points show the complete search history. The red star marks the baseline. The compromise marker will be explained below.

The 2D views are usually easier to read than the 3D view; use them to compare cost and variability at similar annual energy. These plots show the approximate front found by this run, not a guaranteed global front.

In [11]:
baseline_row = comparison.loc["Baseline"].to_dict()
_ = plot_pareto(pareto, evaluated, baseline_row, OUTPUT_DIR / "figures")
plt.show()

10. Choose a design using explicit preferences¶

Optimization supplies alternatives; decision making supplies preferences.

For an illustrative compromise, convert energy to minimization, normalize each objective to 0–1 across the discovered Pareto set, and calculate:

[ score_i = \sqrt{\sum_j w_j z_{ij}^2} ]

A lower score is closer to the ideal point. Equal weights treat the three normalized criteria equally. The ideal combines the best individual objective values and may not be attainable by one design. Rankings depend on the weights and the discovered set's ranges.

This is one transparent preference rule; it does not identify a universally best design.

In [12]:
representatives = representative_designs(pareto)
display(representatives.round(3))

preferences = {
    "Balanced": (1/3, 1/3, 1/3),
    "Energy priority": (0.7, 0.15, 0.15),
    "Cost priority": (0.15, 0.7, 0.15),
    "Stability priority": (0.15, 0.15, 0.7),
}
preferred = pd.DataFrame({
    label: rank_compromises(pareto, weights).iloc[0]
    for label, weights in preferences.items()
}).T

11. Check and export results¶

These checks confirm that the illustrative energy integration and size scaling behave as expected, all searched designs respect the stated bounds, and no reported point is dominated by another evaluated candidate. A fixed seed gives repeatable results with the same weather and software versions.

Tables retain full numerical precision; rounding below is only for display.

In [14]:
# Independent unit check: a constant 2 kW output for 8,760 hours is 17,520 kWh.
constant_power = pd.Series(2.0, index=weather.index)
assert summarize_power(constant_power)["annual_energy_kwh"] == 17520.0
assert summarize_power(constant_power)["daily_cv"] == 0.0

# Check units and scale invariance using the explicit baseline.
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    summarize_power(2 * baseline_ac_kw)["daily_cv"],
    summarize_power(baseline_ac_kw)["daily_cv"],
)
assert (evaluated[DESIGN_COLUMNS].to_numpy() >= LOWER_BOUNDS).all()
assert (evaluated[DESIGN_COLUMNS].to_numpy() <= UPPER_BOUNDS).all()
all_objectives = objective_matrix(evaluated)
for candidate in objective_matrix(pareto):
    dominates = np.all(all_objectives <= candidate, axis=1) & np.any(all_objectives < candidate, axis=1)
    assert not dominates.any()

_ = export_results(
    pareto, evaluated, baseline_row, weather_metadata, OUTPUT_DIR,

)

Interpretation of the supplied run¶

Using the bundled weather, population 40, 30 generations, and seed 42, the search evaluated 1,200 designs and retained 455 nondominated candidates. These recorded values are a reference for the supplied execution; edits to the experiment may change them.

  • The baseline generates 72.30 MWh at an illustrative USD 46,000, with daily CV 0.2047.
  • The equal-weight compromise generates 80.44 MWh at USD 50,125, with daily CV 0.1981: about 11.3% more energy, 9.0% higher cost, and lower relative daily variability.
  • The compromise is larger (56.21 kWp versus 50 kWp). Much of its extra energy comes from added capacity; energy per kWp is slightly lower than the baseline, so this is not an efficiency improvement.
  • The highest-energy candidate generates 148.61 MWh at USD 88,718, with daily CV 0.2060. It gains total energy at substantially higher cost and higher variability than the compromise.
  • The lowest-CV candidate has CV 0.1968 and produces 58.44 MWh. Selecting it gives up total annual generation in exchange for a small reduction in relative daily variability.

The useful choice depends on preferences. These results describe this simplified model and the evaluated candidates, not a globally optimal engineering design.

12. Interpret the result and try small experiments¶

Use the tables and figures to answer:

  1. How much extra energy accompanies the higher investment designs?
  2. Does the orientation with the highest yield also give the lowest daily CV?
  3. How much annual energy changes when variability is prioritized?
  4. What happens to cost and yield when only size changes?
  5. Does increasing generations or changing the random seed alter the approximate front?

Limits of this study: illustrative costs, generic equipment, continuous capacity, one site, fixed DC/AC ratio, a representative weather year, and a modest search budget. No layout/row-spacing model, explicit nearby-object shading, grid constraints, battery dispatch, degradation study, or financial return model is included. The cost and energy objectives are strongly related through size; some trade-offs can therefore be simple. We report the behavior the model produces rather than requiring all objectives to conflict.

For a research extension, use several continuous historical years, distinguish seasonal variation from ramp rates, add layout or budget constraints, validate equipment models, and compare convergence across seeds.
